opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a really interesting question, and I've thought about it a lot because I've actually spent a fair amount of time working on efficient Transformers and alternative architectures myself. The honest answer is that the Transformer is just a really, really good default. It's not perfect, but it hits a sweet spot that is very hard to beat.

Part of it is the hardware lottery idea. The Transformer maps extremely well onto the accelerators we have, TPUs and GPUs, because it's basically big matrix multiplies. So it's not just the architecture by itself, it's the whole ecosystem: the kernels, the compilers, the distributed training infrastructure, all the tricks people have figured out over years. Any new architecture isn't competing against the 2017 Transformer, it's competing against the Transformer plus seven or eight years of collective engineering and optimization. That's a really high bar.

The second thing is that a lot of the alternatives look good at small scale or on specific benchmarks, but when you scale them up they don't hold up as well, or they have some weakness that shows up later, like in-context retrieval or certain kinds of reasoning. Back when we wrote the efficient Transformers survey, there were so many X-formers, and most of them kind of faded because when you actually scaled them, vanilla attention with some tweaks was just more robust. People underestimate how much robustness matters. When you're spending millions of dollars on a training run, you don't want to bet on something that might break in a weird way.

And I think there's also a risk-aversion thing in industry. If you're a big lab, the expected value of switching architecture has to be really high, because you lose all your accumulated knowledge about scaling laws, hyperparameters, and so on. So even if something is slightly better, slightly isn't enough. It has to be dramatically better.

That said, I don't think it's impossible. Things like state space models and hybrids are interesting, and I think the Transformer itself keeps evolving. The Transformer today isn't the exact same thing as the original paper. We changed the normalization, positional embeddings, activation functions, MoE, and so on. So in a way the field has moved beyond the original Transformer, just incrementally rather than through some dramatic replacement.

r001.rationale: The response says Transformers benefit from years of collective engineering and optimization, raising the bar for alternatives.

r002.rationale: It mentions losing accumulated knowledge about scaling laws and hyperparameters, but does not say compatibility with prior ideas constrains which alternatives can succeed.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few things going on. The first is that it's actually really hard to beat the Transformer, and I say that as someone who spent years trying. When I was at Google Brain we did this big study, the "Scaling Laws vs Model Architectures" paper, where we scaled up something like ten different architectures, including a bunch of our own proposed ones, and the honest result was that the vanilla Transformer was basically the most robust thing across scales. A lot of alternatives look great at small scale and then the gap closes or reverses when you scale them up. So part of the reason people haven't moved on is just that nothing has clearly won.

The second thing is the inductive bias question. People love to claim the Transformer has no inductive bias, and I actually think that's a bit of a misconception. Attention is a very specific thing. But it turns out to be a very good general prior for sequence modeling, and it's extremely hardware friendly. The whole stack, TPUs, GPUs, the kernels, the systems people, everyone has co-evolved with this architecture for seven or eight years now. If you come in with a new architecture, you're not just competing with the model, you're competing with the entire ecosystem of optimizations around it. That's a huge moat.

And then the third reason is kind of sociological. Architecture research used to be a thing a grad student could do with a couple of GPUs. Now, to credibly show something beats a Transformer, you need to train at a scale where the result actually matters, and that's really expensive. So the people who can afford to run the experiment are mostly the frontier labs, and they're very risk averse about this, because if you commit to a new architecture for a flagship model and it has some weird failure mode at long context or in instruction following, that's a very costly mistake. So the incentive is to keep the backbone and iterate on data and post-training instead.

I'd also say that a lot of the things that did get adopted, like the hybrid models, state space layers mixed with attention, sliding window stuff, MoE, they got adopted precisely because they're not really "beyond" Transformers. They're modifications that slot into the existing recipe. So I don't think we're stuck forever. I just think the bar for replacing it is extremely high, and the realistic path is incremental evolution rather than some clean new architecture showing up and sweeping everything.

r001.rationale: The response says the Transformer ecosystem—including TPUs, GPUs, kernels, and systems—has co-evolved around the architecture, creating a large moat for alternatives.

r002.rationale: The response explains that adopted alternatives tend to be modifications that slot into the existing Transformer recipe, identifying compatibility with that recipe as a constraint.

astra-6.text:
I think a big part of it is that you’re not just competing with an architecture. You’re competing with an entire ecosystem that has been optimized around that architecture. People know how to train Transformers, the kernels are good, and there’s a lot of accumulated intuition about what works and what doesn’t.

So if you propose something new, you’re usually testing it at a smaller scale, with less tuning and less optimized infrastructure. And then the question is: if it doesn’t beat a Transformer, is that because the architecture is worse, or because we haven’t put the same amount of work into it? That’s quite difficult to disentangle.

There’s also a risk issue. When you’re spending a lot of compute on a training run, you want something you know will work. A promising result at a small scale doesn’t necessarily give you confidence that it will hold up at a much larger scale. So Transformers keep getting the investment, and that investment keeps making them harder to beat.

I don’t think that means we can’t move beyond them. But a new architecture probably needs a very compelling advantage—something that makes people willing to take that risk.

r001.rationale: It says the Transformer ecosystem has been optimized and that continued investment makes Transformers harder to beat.

r002.rationale: It discusses optimized infrastructure, accumulated intuition, and risk, but does not identify compatibility with prior ideas as a constraint on alternatives.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a big part of it is that you’re competing with an entire ecosystem, not just an architecture. We know how to train Transformers, how to scale them, how to make them run efficiently on the hardware we have. There’s a lot of accumulated knowledge there.

So if you come up with a new architecture, even if the idea is promising, you’re often comparing a relatively unoptimized implementation against something people have spent years optimizing. And showing that it works at a small scale doesn’t necessarily convince people that it will work at the scale they care about. But getting to that scale requires a substantial investment.

That creates a chicken-and-egg problem. You need strong results to justify the compute, and you need the compute to establish those results. I don’t think that means we can’t move beyond Transformers. It means the bar is higher than just having a more elegant idea.

r001.rationale: It says people have spent years optimizing Transformers and accumulated knowledge in training, scaling, and efficiency, making new architectures harder to compare.

r002.rationale: It discusses optimization and investment, but does not identify compatibility with prior ideas as a constraint on which alternatives can succeed.
